visits.text: Thousands of prayer flags crack in the wind at Chele La, reached from Paro on a morning drive: it is the highest point you can reach by road in Bhutan, at 3,988 metres, 35 km from Paro and 26 km from Haa. On a clear day, Mount Jomolhari, a sacred peak on the border with Tibet, shows to the north. It is cold even in summer: keep a warm jacket in the car.

activities.text: Ten minutes on foot is enough to feel the altitude at Chele La, so take the short ridge path slowly. It runs between lines of prayer flags above the road, with the Paro valley on one side and the Haa valley on the other. Do not hurry, drink water, and turn back if you feel dizzy. Snow can cover the pass in winter.

visits.text: Painted phalluses on farmhouse walls may surprise you, but around Chimi Lhakhang they are a blessing, not a joke. The temple was built in 1499 and is linked to Drukpa Kunley, a monk nicknamed the Divine Madman, who used the symbol to drive away evil. Villagers believe it protects a house from jealousy and gossip. Couples hoping for a child come here to be blessed. Allow 45 minutes.

activities.text: Rice paddies and mustard fields line the 20-minute footpath from Sopsokha village to Chimi Lhakhang. The track is dusty in dry weather and muddy after rain, so wear closed shoes. Take your time: farmers work the terraces on both sides, and the temple appears on its low hill at the end.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Bhutan in 8 Days: Paro, Thimphu, Punakha and Haa

visits.text: Dochula Pass lines up 108 white chortens (small Buddhist monuments) on a mound at 3,100 metres, on the road from Thimphu to Punakha. A queen mother had them built in 2004 in memory of Bhutanese soldiers killed in a battle in December 2003. On clear days you see the Himalayan peaks, including Gangkhar Puensum, the highest mountain in Bhutan at 7,570 metres. October to February gives the clearest views; bring a jacket.

If clouds hide the mountains, step inside Druk Wangyal Lhakhang, the temple just above the chortens of Dochula Pass. It was completed in 2008 to mark 100 years of the monarchy and honours the fourth king. Every 13 December, masked dancers perform here during the Dochula festival. Fifteen minutes is enough.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Bhutan in 8 Days: Paro, Thimphu, Punakha and Haa

visits.text: One legend says a white pigeon and a black pigeon chose the sites of the two old temples of Haa. Lhakhang Karpo, the White Temple, is where the white one landed. Tradition dates it to the 7th century, in the time of the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo. It stands near the main road, less than a kilometre south of the fortress of Haa. Few tour groups come this far: you may have the courtyard to yourself.

Lhakhang Nagpo, the Black Temple, stands a little above the White Temple of Haa, a few minutes away on foot. Its dark walls give it its name, and tradition gives it the same 7th-century origin as its neighbour. The building is small, so twenty to thirty minutes is enough. Ask your guide whether the caretaker is there to open the door.

activities.text: You stretch your legs along the main street of Haa town, the small seat of the Haa district, beside the Haa Chhu river. The valley lives from farming and yak herding, and it sees far fewer visitors than Paro. Have lunch here before driving back over Chele La: the return to Paro takes about two and a half hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Bhutan in 8 Days: Paro, Thimphu, Punakha and Haa

visits.text: Built from 1649 as a watchtower against invasions from Tibet, Ta Dzong now holds the National Museum of Bhutan. The museum opened in 1968 and keeps more than 3,000 works: bronze statues, paintings and objects covering 1,500 years of Bhutanese history. The tower stands above Rinpung Dzong, so visit the museum first and then walk down to the fortress. Plan a little over one hour.

Wooden planks sound under your feet on the covered bridge that leads up to Rinpung Dzong, the fortress-monastery of Paro. Consecrated in 1646, it houses the monks and the offices of Paro district. Scenes of the 1993 film Little Buddha were shot in its courtyards. During the Paro festival in March or April, a giant thangka (a painted religious scroll) is unrolled before dawn on the last day. Allow 75 minutes.

Small and easy to drive past, Dungtse Lhakhang deserves twenty minutes on your way through Paro. It is the work of Thangtong Gyalpo, the same 15th-century saint who built the iron bridge at Tachog Lhakhang, seen on your first day. The temple is not always open, so ask your guide to check before you stop.

You pass two orange trees in the courtyard before entering Kyichu Lhakhang, a temple founded in 659, a short drive north of Paro town. Tradition says the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo built 108 temples in a single day to pin down a demoness, and that this is one of them. People believe the two trees bear fruit all year. A second temple was added beside it in 1971. Go before 4.30 pm, when visits end.

activities.text: You land at Paro International Airport, Bhutan's international airport, between steep forested slopes. Your guide waits outside arrivals: a licensed guide must accompany every visitor at all times, including on the road from the airport. You can book the guide, the car and the hotels yourself or through a local tour operator, and apply for the visa online (US$40). Bhutan also charges a Sustainable Development Fee of US$100 per adult per night, a rate extended until 31 December 2029. Keep your visa papers at hand for immigration.

Paro town keeps a main street of traditional two-storey houses with painted wooden windows. An evening walk here is the easy way to end a day of temples: small shops sell textiles, prayer flags and snacks. Go around 5 pm, when schoolchildren and office workers are out. Shops accept ngultrum, the local currency, and often Indian rupees.

If your flight leaves in the morning, your guide takes you straight to Paro International Airport, a few minutes from the centre of Paro. Flights here depend on the weather, so keep the rest of the day free of tight connections. Have your passport and visa papers ready before you reach the terminal.

places.name: Phobjikha

visits.text: Gangtey Goemba is reason enough for the long drive: this monastery (goemba) sits on a spur above the wide Phobjikha Valley, at about 3,000 metres. A grandson of the Buddhist master Pema Lingpa founded it in 1613, and it was fully restored between 2002 and 2008. Walk around the courtyard to see the carved and painted woodwork. Dress warmly: mornings and evenings are cold here even in summer.

Villagers say the cranes circle the monastery three times when they arrive, and three times again when they leave. At the Black-Necked Crane Information Centre in Phobjikha, you learn why these rare birds fly in from the Tibetan Plateau in late October and stay until mid-February. To protect them, power lines in the valley were buried underground. Come in November for the best chance of seeing them: the crane festival is held on 11 November at Gangtey Goemba.

activities.text: You start the Gangtey Nature Trail at the mani wall, a wall of stones carved with prayers, just north of Gangtey Goemba. The path goes gently downhill for about 90 minutes, through pine forest and open meadows, to the small temple of Khewang Lhakhang on the valley floor. It is an easy walk, but you are at 3,000 metres: go slowly and carry water. Ask your driver to wait at the end of the trail.

visits.text: Punakha Dzong sits exactly where two rivers meet, the Pho Chhu and the Mo Chhu, and you enter by a covered wooden bridge. Built in 1637 and 1638, this fortress-monastery was the seat of government until 1955, and every king of Bhutan since 1907 has been crowned here. The senior monks still move in for the winter, because Punakha is warmer than Thimphu. In spring, jacaranda trees flower mauve along the walls. Allow 90 minutes for the three courtyards.

More than 150 metres long, the Punakha Suspension Bridge crosses the Pho Chhu river a short walk from Punakha Dzong. It sways as you walk, and prayer flags are tied along both sides. Villagers use it every day to reach the far bank. Cross slowly, hold the cable if heights bother you, and keep to one side to let people pass.

Save Sangchhen Dorji Lhuendrup Lhakhang for your last morning in Punakha: this nunnery is on the Lobesa side of the valley, on your road out towards Thimphu. About 120 nuns study here, and they also learn embroidery, statue making and religious painting. The temple holds a bronze statue of Avalokiteshvara, the Buddhist figure of compassion, more than 4 metres high. From the ridge you look over three valleys. Stay quiet in the courtyards: classes are in progress.

activities.text: If you have energy for one walk in Punakha, choose Khamsum Yulley Namgyal Chorten. From a footbridge over the Mo Chhu, north of town, the path climbs for about 45 minutes through rice fields and then pine trees. A queen mother had this four-storey monument built in 2004 to protect the country and bring peace. Climb to the roof for the view down the river valley. Start early: the slope is in full sun by late morning.

You board the raft at the bridge below Khamsum Yulley Namgyal Chorten, right after the walk, for the Mo Chhu rafting run. The river carries you about 9 km through gentle rapids, rated easy to moderate, and you land on a sandy beach under the walls of Punakha Dzong. Count 1 to 1.5 hours on the water. Rafting cannot be booked on the spot: ask your guide to arrange it a day ahead. Spring and autumn give the best water levels.

visits.text: Local people say a demoness hid in a rock here, and that Simtokha Dzong was built to hold her down: the name joins the words for demoness and stone. Raised in 1629 by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, the leader who unified Bhutan, it was the first fortress-monastery of its kind in the country. Today it houses a school of Dzongkha, the national language. It lies 5 km south of Thimphu, on your way back to Paro.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Bhutan in 8 Days: Paro, Thimphu, Punakha and Haa

visits.text: Prayer flags snap in the wind above the Paro Chhu river as you cross the iron-chain footbridge to Tachog Lhakhang, a small private temple (lhakhang means temple). Thangtong Gyalpo, a 15th-century saint remembered as the Iron Bridge Builder, founded it, and his descendants still run it. A flood destroyed the bridge in 1969; it was rebuilt in 2005. Allow 30 to 45 minutes: the temple is a 10-minute walk from the highway.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Bhutan in 8 Days: Paro, Thimphu, Punakha and Haa

visits.text: Built in 1692 around a cave where Guru Padmasambhava is said to have meditated, Taktsang monastery stands at 3,120 metres. Legend says this master, who brought Buddhism to Bhutan, flew here on the back of a tigress: hence the name Tiger's Nest. A fire destroyed the main building in 1998 and it was rebuilt by 2005. Inside, four temples are linked by steps cut into the rock. The entry fee is Nu 1,000 per adult; no photos inside.

Rebuilt, repainted and still a question mark: Drukgyel Dzong stands at the head of the Paro valley, half an hour above town. The fortress was raised in 1649 to celebrate a victory over an invasion from Tibet, then burned in the early 1950s. It has been rebuilt since 2016, but no official source says whether the interior is open. It is a short drive beyond the Taktsang trailhead: stop for a photo from outside after your hike.

activities.text: If you do only one hike in Bhutan, make it the trail to Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest. The monastery hangs on a cliff about 900 metres above the Paro valley, and the path climbs steadily through pine forest. Count 5 to 6 hours in total: about 4 hours of walking, up and down, plus an hour inside the monastery. A cafeteria at the halfway viewpoint lets you rest with the monastery in sight. After it, stone steps go down to a waterfall and a bridge, then up again. Start by 8 am, then drive back to Paro for the night.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Bhutan in 8 Days: Paro, Thimphu, Punakha and Haa

visits.text: At 54 metres, the gilded bronze Buddha Dordenma watches over the southern entrance to Thimphu from its hilltop. Completed in 2015, the seated statue holds more than 100,000 small Buddha figures inside, each one gilded like the giant itself. Go early, before the tour groups, when the terrace is quiet and you can look down on the whole valley. Walk around the base clockwise, as Buddhists do, and keep shoulders and knees covered.

Prayer wheels turn all day at the Memorial Chorten, a white monument with a golden spire in the middle of Thimphu (a chorten is a Buddhist monument, also called a stupa). It was built in 1974 in memory of the third king, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, on the initiative of his mother. Unlike most monuments of this kind, it holds no human remains, only a photograph of the king. Join the residents who walk around it clockwise: twenty minutes is enough.

If you turn up at midday, you will find Tashichho Dzong closed: on working days it opens to visitors only from about 5 pm, once the offices empty. A dzong is a fortress that serves as both monastery and government building. This one holds the throne room and the offices of the king, and the country's senior monks spend the summer in its northern wing. The present building dates from the 1960s. Wear long sleeves and ask your guide to confirm the hours that day.

You climb to Changangkha Lhakhang alongside parents carrying newborns: this hilltop temple above Thimphu is where families ask for the protection of their children. It was founded in the 13th century, which makes it one of the old temples of the valley. Inside, the main statue shows Avalokiteshvara, the Buddhist figure of compassion, with eleven heads. Spin the prayer wheels along the outer wall, then pause in the courtyard for the view over the city.

Odd-looking is the kind way to describe the takin, and the Motithang Takin Preserve is the easy place to see one. Bhutan's national animal has the body of a cow and the face of a goat; legend says a 15th-century saint, Drukpa Kunley, created it by joining the bones of both. The fenced forest was once a small zoo, closed by order of the king, but the animals refused to leave town. Allow 45 minutes and walk the fence path slowly.

The National Textile Museum, part of the Royal Textile Academy, explains why Bhutanese cloth is treated as an art. Opened in 2001, it displays weaving and embroidery from past centuries to today, including crowns and clothes worn by the kings. Across the courtyard, weavers work at their looms and you can watch them. Photography is not allowed inside. The museum is open Monday to Saturday, 9 am to 4 pm: plan one hour.

It looks like an ordinary farmhouse, yet the Folk Heritage Museum is the quickest way to understand how rural Bhutanese families lived. The traditional house is furnished with farm tools, kitchen utensils and household objects, floor by floor. It stands a few hundred metres from the National Institute for Zorig Chusum, so visit both in the same morning. Weekday hours are 10.30 am to 4.30 pm, shorter at weekends.

activities.text: You walk through working classrooms at the National Institute for Zorig Chusum, the state school of the thirteen traditional crafts of Bhutan. Students spend years learning painting, wood carving, embroidery, sculpture or silverwork: the same skills that built and decorated every dzong and temple on your route. Visitors move quietly from room to room while classes go on. Come on a weekday in term time, and ask before taking photos of students.

Dried chillies, incense sticks and blocks of hard cheese fill the stalls of the Centenary Farmers' Market, the busiest food market in Thimphu, near the Wang Chhu river. The building was renovated and reopened in September 2023. Head upstairs for incense and chugo, a dried cheese so hard that people suck it like a sweet for hours. Many residents still call it the weekend market: Saturday and Sunday are the liveliest days.

Skip the hotel gift shop: the Craft Bazaar in central Thimphu is a simpler place to buy handicrafts made in Bhutan. The stalls sell woven cloth, wooden bowls and handmade paper, and an evening stroll here is a gentle way to end the day. Prices are usually displayed, so there is little bargaining. Ask your guide which stalls sell locally made pieces rather than imports.

visits.text: Founded in 1638, burned to the ground in 2012, consecrated again in 2022: Wangdue Phodrang Dzong has had a second life. The fortress-monastery stands on a ridge above the Punatsangchhu river and houses both district offices and monks. No visiting hours are published, and what is open changes from day to day. Let your guide check before you stop; a small entry fee applies to foreign visitors.
